## <span class="num">11.5.1</span> The Statements

By Lagrange’s theorem, the order of a subgroup of $G$ divides $|G|$. The converse fails: a divisor of $|G|$ need not be the order of any subgroup.

:::example{11.5.1} Missing subgroups
A subgroup of index 2 contains every element of odd order (Lemma [11.2.6](/notes/math-55a/11-2-conjugation-and-the-class-equation#lemma-11-2-6)). So a subgroup of order 6 in $A_4$ would contain the identity and the eight 3-cycles, and a subgroup of order 30 in $A_5$ would contain the identity, the twenty 3-cycles and the twenty-four 5-cycles. Both are impossible: $A_4$ has no subgroup of order 6, and $A_5$ has no subgroup of order 30.
:::

The Sylow theorems show that the converse does hold for prime powers, and they say much more.

:::definition{11.5.2} Sylow $p$-subgroup
Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ a prime, and write $|G| = p^e m$ with $p \nmid m$. A ***Sylow $p$-subgroup*** of $G$ is a subgroup of order $p^e$. A ***$p$-subgroup*** of $G$ is a subgroup that is a $p$-group.
:::

:::theorem{11.5.3} The Sylow Theorems (Sylow, 1872)
Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ a prime, and write $|G| = p^e m$ with $p \nmid m$.

<!-- list:paren-decimal -->

1. $G$ has a Sylow $p$-subgroup.
2. Any two Sylow $p$-subgroups $H$ and $H'$ of $G$ are conjugate: $H' = gHg^{-1}$ for some $g \in G$. More generally, every $p$-subgroup of $G$ is contained in a Sylow $p$-subgroup.
3. The number $s_p$ of Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$ satisfies $s_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ and $s_p \mid m$.
:::

We prove these theorems in Section [11.5.3](/notes/math-55a/11-5-the-sylow-theorems). When $p \nmid |G|$ they are trivial ($e = 0$, and $\{e\}$ is the only Sylow $p$-subgroup), so the interesting case is $p \mid |G|$. A few remarks:

- Since $s_p \equiv 1 \pmod p$, $s_p$ is prime to $p$, so $s_p \mid m$ is equivalent to $s_p \mid |G|$.
- A conjugate of a Sylow $p$-subgroup is again a Sylow $p$-subgroup. So by (2), a Sylow $p$-subgroup $H$ is normal if and only if it is the only one, that is, $s_p = 1$: if $s_p = 1$ then $gHg^{-1} = H$ for all $g$, and if $H$ is normal then every Sylow $p$-subgroup, being conjugate to $H$, equals $H$.

:::corollary{11.5.4} Cauchy’s theorem
If $p$ is a prime dividing $|G|$, then $G$ contains an element of order $p$.
:::

:::proof
By Sylow’s first theorem, $G$ has a subgroup $H$ of order $p^e \geq p$. Pick $g \in H$, $g \neq e$. The order of $g$ divides $|H| = p^e$, so it is $p^k$ for some $1 \leq k \leq e$. Then $g^{p^{k-1}}$ has order $p$.
:::

:::note
For a $p$-group $G$ the Sylow theorems say nothing: the only Sylow $p$-subgroup is $G$ itself. In the Sylow approach to classifying finite groups the $p$-groups are therefore the hardest case, and their number grows very fast with the exponent. For $p = 2$:

<div class="table-wrap"><table class="tex-table has-stub"><thead><tr><th scope="col" class="l">order</th><th scope="col" class="c">$2$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$4$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$8$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$16$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$32$</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row" class="l">number of groups</th><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">2</td><td class="c">5</td><td class="c">14</td><td class="c">51</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

(order 4 is Corollary [11.2.5](/notes/math-55a/11-2-conjugation-and-the-class-equation#corollary-11-2-5) and order 8 is Proposition [11.2.7](/notes/math-55a/11-2-conjugation-and-the-class-equation#proposition-11-2-7)), and there are already 56092 groups of order $2^8 = 256$.
:::

## <span class="num">11.5.2</span> Normalizers and Conjugate Subgroups

A group $G$ acts by conjugation on the set of its subgroups, $g \cdot H = gHg^{-1}$. The orbit of $H$ is the set of subgroups conjugate to $H$, and $H$ is normal exactly when this orbit is $\{H\}$.

:::definition{11.5.5} Normalizer
The ***normalizer*** of a subgroup $H \leq G$ is $$N_G(H) = \{g \in G : gHg^{-1} = H\},$$ the stabilizer of $H$ for the conjugation action on subgroups. We write $N(H)$ when $G$ is clear.
:::

As a stabilizer, $N_G(H)$ is a subgroup of $G$, and it contains $H$. For a subgroup $K$ with $H \leq K \leq G$, $H$ is normal in $K$ if and only if $kHk^{-1} = H$ for all $k \in K$, that is, if and only if $K \subseteq N_G(H)$. So $N_G(H)$ is the largest subgroup of $G$ in which $H$ is normal, and $H \trianglelefteq G$ if and only if $N_G(H) = G$. The normalizer measures how far $H$ is from being normal.

:::example{11.5.6} Normalizers in $S_3$
Let $\sigma = (1\,2\,3)$ and $\tau = (1\,2)$. The subgroup $A_3 = \{e, \sigma, \sigma^2\}$ is normal, so $N(A_3) = S_3$, even though $\tau$ does not commute with $\sigma$: $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1} = (2\,1\,3) = \sigma^2$. Conjugation by $\tau$ moves the elements of $A_3$ but preserves the subgroup. On the other hand, for $H = \{e, \tau\}$ we have $gHg^{-1} = \{e, g\tau g^{-1}\}$, which equals $H$ if and only if $g$ commutes with $\tau$; the centralizer of $\tau$ has $6/3 = 2$ elements, so $N(H) = \{e, \tau\} = H$.
:::

:::proposition{11.5.7} Counting conjugate subgroups
The number of subgroups of $G$ conjugate to $H$ is $[G : N_G(H)]$.
:::

:::proof
These subgroups form the orbit of $H$ for the conjugation action, whose stabilizer is $N_G(H)$. Apply the Orbit–Stabilizer Theorem.
:::

## <span class="num">11.5.3</span> Proofs of the Sylow Theorems

Fix a finite group $G$ and a prime $p$, and write $|G| = n = p^e m$ with $p \nmid m$. The first two theorems are proved by letting $G$ act on suitable sets by left multiplication, and the third by letting a Sylow subgroup act by conjugation.

:::lemma{11.5.8} A binomial coefficient
If $n = p^e m$ with $p \nmid m$, then $p \nmid \binom{n}{p^e}$.
:::

:::proof
We have $$\binom{n}{p^e} = \frac{n(n-1) \cdots (n - p^e + 1)}{p^e(p^e - 1) \cdots 1} = \prod_{k=0}^{p^e - 1} \frac{p^e m - k}{p^e - k}.$$ The factor for $k = 0$ is $m$, which is prime to $p$. For $0 < k < p^e$, write $k = p^a k'$ with $p \nmid k'$; then $a < e$, and $$p^e m - k = p^a (p^{e-a} m - k'), \qquad p^e - k = p^a (p^{e-a} - k'),$$ where neither $p^{e-a}m - k'$ nor $p^{e-a} - k'$ is divisible by $p$, since both are congruent to $-k'$ modulo $p$. So the numerator and the denominator of each factor are divisible by exactly the same power of $p$. Hence the power of $p$ in the numerator of the product equals the power of $p$ in its denominator, and the integer $\binom{n}{p^e}$ is not divisible by $p$.
:::

:::lemma{11.5.9} Stabilizers of subsets
Let $G$ act on the set of its subsets by left multiplication, $g \cdot U = gU$. For every subset $U \subseteq G$, $|\Stab(U)|$ divides $|U|$.
:::

:::proof
Let $H = \Stab(U) = \{g \in G : gU = U\}$. Then $hu \in U$ for all $h \in H$ and $u \in U$, so $H$ acts on $U$ by left multiplication. The orbit of $u \in U$ is the right coset $Hu$, which has $|H|$ elements. Since $U$ is the disjoint union of these orbits, $|H|$ divides $|U|$.
:::

:::proof Proof of the First Sylow Theorem
Let $S$ be the set of all subsets of $G$ with $p^e$ elements, so $|S| = \binom{n}{p^e}$. Left multiplication preserves the number of elements of a subset, so $G$ acts on $S$ by $g \cdot U = gU$. By Lemma [11.5.8](/notes/math-55a/11-5-the-sylow-theorems#lemma-11-5-8), $p \nmid |S|$. Since $|S|$ is the sum of the sizes of the orbits, some orbit $G \cdot U$ has $p \nmid |G \cdot U|$. Now $|G| = |G \cdot U| \cdot |\Stab(U)|$ is divisible by $p^e$, and $p \nmid |G \cdot U|$, so $p^e$ divides $|\Stab(U)|$. On the other hand $|\Stab(U)|$ divides $|U| = p^e$ by Lemma [11.5.9](/notes/math-55a/11-5-the-sylow-theorems#lemma-11-5-9). So $|\Stab(U)| = p^e$, and $\Stab(U)$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup. (In fact $U$ is then a single orbit of $\Stab(U)$, that is, a right coset of $\Stab(U)$.)
:::

:::proof Proof of the Second Sylow Theorem
Let $H$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup, which exists by the first theorem, and let $K$ be a $p$-subgroup of $G$. Let $G$ act on the set $G/H$ of left cosets of $H$ by left multiplication; $|G/H| = m$ is not divisible by $p$. Restrict this action to $K$. The size of each $K$-orbit divides $|K|$, so it is a power of $p$. Since $p \nmid m$ and $m$ is the sum of the sizes of the $K$-orbits, some orbit has size $p^0 = 1$: there is a coset $gH$ with $kgH = gH$ for all $k \in K$. Then $g^{-1}kg \in H$, that is, $k \in gHg^{-1}$, for every $k \in K$. So $K \subseteq gHg^{-1}$, which is a Sylow $p$-subgroup, since it has the same order as $H$. If $K$ is itself a Sylow $p$-subgroup, then $|K| = |gHg^{-1}|$ and $K = gHg^{-1}$.
:::

:::proof Proof of the Third Sylow Theorem
Let $G$ act by conjugation on the set of its Sylow $p$-subgroups. By the second theorem this action is transitive, and the stabilizer of a Sylow $p$-subgroup $H$ is $N(H)$, so $s_p = |G|/|N(H)|$ (Proposition [11.5.7](/notes/math-55a/11-5-the-sylow-theorems#proposition-11-5-7)). Since $H \leq N(H)$, $|N(H)| = p^e t$ for some integer $t$, and $s_p = p^e m/(p^e t) = m/t$ divides $m$.

Now restrict the conjugation action to $H$. The orbit of $H$ itself is $\{H\}$. We claim that it is the only orbit of size 1. Suppose $H'$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup with $hH'h^{-1} = H'$ for all $h \in H$, that is, $H \subseteq N(H')$. The order of $N(H')$ is a multiple of $|H'| = p^e$ and divides $|G| = p^e m$, so $p^e$ is the largest power of $p$ dividing $|N(H')|$, and $H$ and $H'$ are Sylow $p$-subgroups of $N(H')$. By the second theorem applied to the group $N(H')$, $H = xH'x^{-1}$ for some $x \in N(H')$. But $xH'x^{-1} = H'$ by the definition of $N(H')$, so $H = H'$. This proves the claim.

Every orbit of the $H$-action has size dividing $|H| = p^e$, so every orbit other than $\{H\}$ has size divisible by $p$. Since $s_p$ is the sum of the sizes of the orbits, $s_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$.
:::
